‘Not everyone would have persisted so kindly and refused to accept Jane’s answer. But yesterday she firmly declared that she would not write the refusal Jane wanted her to send. She would wait—and sure enough, by yesterday evening everything was arranged for Jane to go. It came as a complete surprise to me! I had no idea at all. Jane took Mrs. Elton aside and told her straight away that, after considering the advantages of the position with Mrs. Smallridge, she had decided to accept it. I knew nothing about it until it was all settled.’

‘You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton?’

‘Yes, all of us. Mrs. Elton insisted. We arranged it on the hill while we were walking with Mr. Knightley. “You must all spend the evening with us,” she said. “I absolutely insist on having every one of you.”’

‘Was Mr. Knightley there as well?’

‘No, he wasn’t. He declined from the start. I thought he might come, since Mrs. Elton said she wouldn’t let him off, but he didn’t. My mother, Jane, and I were all there, though, and we had a very pleasant evening. One must always enjoy the company of such kind friends, you know, Miss Woodhouse, although everyone seemed rather tired after the morning’s outing. Even pleasure can be exhausting, you know, and I can’t say any of them seemed to have enjoyed it very much. Still, I shall always remember it as a very pleasant party, and feel extremely grateful to the kind friends who invited me.’

‘I suppose Miss Fairfax had been reaching her decision throughout the day, though you didn’t realise it?’

‘I expect she had.’

‘Whenever she has to leave, it must be painful for her and all her friends. But I hope everything possible will make the position easier—I mean the family’s character and behaviour.’

‘Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, indeed, everything is there to make her happy. Apart from the Sucklings and Bragges, Mrs. Elton knows no family with such generous and elegant arrangements for their children. Mrs. Smallridge is a delightful woman! Their way of life is almost equal to Maple Grove’s. And as for the children, except for the little Sucklings and the little Bragges, you won’t find such charming, refined children anywhere. Jane will be treated with such consideration and kindness! It will be one pleasure after another, a life full of pleasure. And her salary! I really couldn’t bring myself to tell you the amount, Miss Woodhouse.’

At the head of the stairs he regained his composure and decided to utter his celebrated burst of demoniacal laughter. He had found this exceedingly effective on several previous occasions. It was reputed to have whitened Lord Raker’s wig in the course of one night, and had certainly caused three French governesses of Lady Canterville’s to give notice before completing their first month. Accordingly, he laughed his most appalling laugh, until the ancient vaulted ceiling echoed again and again. Scarcely had the dreadful reverberation faded, however, when a door opened and Mrs. Otis appeared in a pale blue dressing-gown. ‘I fear you are quite unwell,’ she said, ‘so I have brought some of Dr. Dobell’s tincture. If you are suffering from indigestion, it is an admirable cure.’ The ghost stared furiously at her and immediately prepared to transform himself into a great black dog, a feat for which he was deservedly famous, and to which the family physician invariably ascribed the lasting idiocy of Lord Canterville’s uncle, the Hon. Thomas Horton. But approaching footsteps checked his sinister intention. He merely allowed himself to grow faintly phosphorescent, and disappeared with a profound sepulchral groan just as the twins reached him.

Once in his room, he broke down altogether and surrendered to violent agitation. Naturally, the twins’ vulgarity and Mrs. Otis’s blatant materialism were exceedingly vexing; yet his greatest sorrow was his failure to wear the armour. He had trusted that the spectacle of a Spectre In Armour would move even modern Americans, if on no more rational grounds than respect for their national poet, Longfellow. He himself had passed many a tiresome hour over that poet’s graceful, pleasing verses while the Cantervilles were in town. Moreover, the armour belonged to him. He had worn it to great effect at the Kenilworth tournament, receiving warm compliments from no less a personage than the Virgin Queen. Yet, upon putting it on this time, he had been utterly overcome by the massive breastplate and steel helmet. He had crashed onto the stone paving, badly scraping both knees and bruising his right-hand knuckles.

For several days afterwards he was seriously unwell, scarcely leaving his room except to maintain the blood-stain in proper condition. By looking after himself with the utmost care, however, he recovered, and determined upon a third endeavour to terrify the United States Minister and his family.

After delivering them, I found it impossible to stay away from the places that held them. I felt as though my presence made their prospects brighter and less hopeless. In this senseless agitation and distress I wandered the streets at evening, passing the offices and houses where I had deposited my petitions. Even now, the dreary western streets of London on a chilly, dusty spring night, their ranks of stern, shuttered mansions and long lines of lamps, sadden me because of that remembrance.

My daily visits to him were now briefer, and he was watched more closely. Observing, or imagining, that I was suspected of wishing to bring him poison, I requested a search before taking my seat beside his bed. I told the officer who remained constantly present that I would do anything to convince him of the innocence of my intentions. Neither he nor I was treated unkindly. There was a duty to perform, and it was performed without severity. The officer invariably told me that he had grown worse. The other sick prisoners in the room, and those prisoners tending them as nurses—criminals, yet not beyond kindness, thank God!—always confirmed that report.

With each passing day I saw more clearly how quietly he lay gazing at the white ceiling, his face without brightness until something I said briefly lit it, after which it faded once more. At times he could scarcely speak, or could not speak at all; then a faint pressure of his hand upon mine served as his reply, and I learned to interpret it very well.

Ten days had elapsed when I found him more greatly altered than ever before. His eyes were fixed upon the doorway and brightened when I came in.

‘Dear boy,’ he said as I seated myself beside him, ‘I thought you was behind time. But I knowed you couldn’t be.’

‘It is exactly the hour,’ I answered. ‘I waited at the gate until it came.’

‘You always waits by the gate, dear boy, don’t you?’

‘Yes, so that we need not lose a moment.’

‘Thank’ee, dear boy, thank’ee. God bless you! You never abandoned me, dear boy.’

I squeezed his hand without speaking, unable to forget that I had once intended to abandon him.

‘And the best thing of all,’ he went on, ‘is that you’ve felt easier alonger me since I’ve been beneath a dark cloud than you did when the sun was shining.’
